title: Building a Rural House under QCVN 01:2026: Site Choice, 6 m Setback
desc: QCVN 01:2026 from 2027 for rural houses: where residential land is barred, the 6 m setback from inter-commune roads, plots with gardens, and livestock waste.
summary: The requirements of QCVN 01:2026/BXD on rural planning that bear directly on building a house in a commune: site choice, setback from inter-commune roads, house plots and building density.
body: p

Part 4 of QCVN 01:2026/BXD (issued with Circular 46/2026/TT-BXD, effective from 1 January 2027) sets technical rules for rural planning. It is the basis on which authorities prepare commune master plans and detailed plans for residential areas; people building a house in a commune should know it to choose land and design appropriately.
h2
1. Where residential land cannot be placed
p
Under section 4.1, land for rural construction must have secure natural conditions. Planning must not allocate civil land:
ul
In areas at risk of dangerous geological hazards, areas that are frequently flooded or hit by flash floods and torrents; in coastal and estuary areas, rising sea level must be taken into account;
In areas already designated for mining, nature conservation, archaeological sites, or polluted areas that have not been treated.
p
Planning must minimise the use of farmland, especially high-yield land, and make use of hills, mounds, riverbanks and poor farmland to expand residential areas.
h2
2. Houses fronting inter-commune roads: minimum 6 m setback
p

New rural civil land must not be placed right next to inter-commune roads or higher. For existing residential areas running along roads of inter-commune level or above, a minimum setback of 6 m from the boundary of the road's safety corridor must be ensured (section 4.4.2.9). New rural residential areas also must not be placed adjacent to the safety corridor of expressways, national highways, provincial roads or inter-commune roads (section 4.4.2.1).
p
Before buying roadside land to build a house, ask the commune People's Committee about the road safety corridor boundary and the setback that applies.
h2
3. What does a rural house plot include?
ul
The basic functions of a rural house plot comprise land for building the house and agricultural land attached to the house (garden, pond, etc.) (section 4.5.2.3).
The plot area must reasonably arrange these functions, suited to natural conditions and the common landscape (section 4.5.2.4).
Production and livestock buildings within the plot must have a waste collection and treatment system that ensures environmental hygiene (section 4.5.2.5).
At planning level, average rural residential land must be not less than 25 m² per person, excluding agricultural land attached to the house (Table 28).
h2
4. Building density: garden land counts
p

Table 8 sets the maximum net building density of a private house plot by plot area: ≤ 90 m²: 100%; 100 m²: 90%; 200 m²: 70%; 300 m²: 60%; 500 m²: 50%; ≥ 1,000 m²: 40%. For a rural house plot with agricultural land attached to the house, the plot area includes both the house land and the agricultural land attached to the house (note 2 to Table 8, section 2.5.3.1).
p

For example: a 500 m² plot comprising residential land and garden has a maximum density under Table 8 of 50%, meaning the footprint of the buildings must not exceed 250 m². Specific indicators are set by the commune's planning.
h2
5. Rural house architecture
p

Rural house models must be arranged reasonably, suited to natural conditions, landscape and local architectural traditions, with local materials encouraged (note 3 to Table 28). Planning must allow continuation of the traditional settlement structure and preserve existing architectural and landscape values (section 4.4.2.5).
p

On procedure: many rural houses are exempt from a permit if they are not in an area that already has planning – see Which private houses are exempt from a construction permit; for splitting a plot to build a house see Conditions for splitting and merging land plots.
note

This article is only a summary for reference and does not replace the legal texts. QCVN 01:2026/BXD takes effect from 1 January 2027; plans approved before this date continue to be implemented until their term ends (section 5.4.1). Specific indicators for each plot follow the commune master plan and detailed plan; ask the commune People's Committee before building.
